note:
v1, IN THE TIME OF (track nine, whole-song skeleton). The drum pulse never leaves 84. Two guitars teach seven strokes slowly: open F, mute, mute, answer, mute, answer, mute. Each seven bars the space between strokes shrinks: one per beat, then two, three, four, five and six. Before seven, the head of the cell meets a quarter only once in seven beats. The two pitch answers alternate; the articulation repeats in seven strokes, the pitches in fourteen.
At five and six (1:20–2:00) the guitars thin to two and a short F4 tap marks each cell head. Its two custom wavetable frames come from the riff: harmonics 1/4/6 from the open notes, 2/3/5/7 from the muted ones. At 2:00 the tap gives its job to the kick and bass: seven guitar strokes now fit one quarter, six guitars play them, and the rhythm section walks. At 2:40 the slow seven strokes return as chords. 3:06 written, 3:11 with the tail.

v14, FIVE, COUNTED BY HAND (section w4, 1:20.0–1:30.0, the first two turns of the fives; my last note called them the least worked stretch). 'Five in the time of four' is how a musician says a quintuplet; in North India it is a tala. A TABLA plays jhaptal, the ten-beat cycle, at five strokes to the beat: dhin na | dhin dhin na, tin na | dhin dhin na. Its two-and-three fall inside every beat of the kit. Its ten strokes last two beats, so the bass drum of the pair sounds on one and three and is left out on two and four, where the snare is. Three things now turn at once: the kit in four, the tabla in ten, the riff in seven; the riff's head and its tap land on a different bol each time (first, third, fifth, second, fourth). The last two beats are a tihai, the thrice-said cadence: te re dha three times with a stroke's rest between, so a dha every fourth stroke of five. Its last dha is the beat where the tap begins its tune (v6): the five places in the beat are counted by a drum, then the tap gives each a pitch. The kit, guitars, bass and tap do not change. New sound: it-tabla, the library tabla-kit (no other song on the record uses it), treble drum on F4, bass drum on the riff's F2.

LISTEN FOR 0:00: under the two clean guitars playing the slow tune there is a small wooden tick, tock, one to the beat, where the hat was; at 0:20 the hat is heard for the first time, with the amps, the bass and the kick. Not checked by ear; everything below is written or measured.
WHY. The song is In the Time Of, and what it does is deal one tune out against a beat that never changes. Its first twenty seconds are that beat and that tune and nothing else (two clean guitars since v25), and the beat was kept by the one sound every song on the album has. A clock says what the beat is. Tick and tock alternate, two to the riff's seven, so the tune comes round on the tick one time and on the tock the next: the song's first two-against-seven, before any guitar plays it. And 'two' had no sound of its own (three has the cross bell, four the baritone and the clavinet, five the tabla, six the six-string, seven the rupak): now the hat is its arrival.
THE PATCH, it-clock (song-local, a kit of two pieces): each a struck bar, a sine with partials at 2.76 and 5.4 times (-8 and -14 dB) and a 3 ms click of noise on the front; ti on C7 (2093 Hz, decay 60 ms), to on F6 (1397 Hz, the song's key note, 90 ms); no humanising (a clock); a small room (0.4 s, 12%); centre, fader -17 dB. The hat's 28 strokes in the section become ti on the even beats and to on the odd, 0.3 over the hat's velocities; the hat keeps its other 58.
MEASURED, raw, the opening. Whole (K): the clock -43.0 dB where the hat stood -42.6 (the clean pair -30.3): the level was fitted to that. A stroke's first 60 ms against the pair's same 60 ms: tick -5.1, tock -4.6 (the hat -6.7): shorter strokes, so more of them is in the front. They ring 34 and 68 ms to 20 dB down (the hat 84). The tick has 81% of its energy at 2-4 kHz (centroid 2.9 kHz), the tock 83% at 1-2 kHz (1.9 kHz); the hat had 96% above 4 kHz. (Read from a bench 2 dB louder, scaled.) FINISHED, the opening against v26 by band: +1.1 dB at 1-2 kHz, +1.0 at 2-4 kHz, -0.4 at 4-8 kHz and -13.0 at 8-16 kHz; its level -24.4 > -24.3 K. Every other section within 0.006 dB, four untouched stretches with -67 to -73 dB left after matching; the loudness target is not moved.
SCORES seeds 0/11: 94.565 / 94.363 against 94.545 / 93.963.
THE COST: the opening has almost nothing above 8 kHz now (the hat's hiss was all of it); the top arrives at 0:20 with the hat and the amps. WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether it reads as a clock or as a woodblock or a metronome; whether a clock at the head of a djent song is charming or coy; whether tick and tock a fifth apart sound like a tune. 29 of 29 older switches off still give what v26's generator gives; C10T9_CLOCK='' is v26 byte for byte.

The same six strings, the same tuning, every stroke where it was; no note changes and no other part is touched. Not checked by ear; everything below is measured or reasoned. LISTEN FOR 1:40-1:50: under the sextuplets a string enters, then two, then three, until one pass across six strings fills every beat; it should buzz and sing now where it was a soft thrum under the guitars, and stop at 1:50 where the cadence starts. HOW IT WAS CHOSEN: AN AUDIT OF THE GUESTS. Every speed in this song has a guest of its own (v13's words). I rendered each alone and read it against everything else while it sounds (raw, K-weighted, seed 0). Under everything else by: the clock 9.3; the open hat 11.5 (but it is all of the top octave); the ride bell 5.9; the baritone 6.1 and the clavinet 5.0; the tap 5.3 in the fives and 8.4 in the sixes; the tabla 5.1 in the fives, 8.7 in the lock; the organ 8.9; and THE SIX STRINGS 11.1, the lowest of the pitched guests, holding no band of the passage (19% at 250 Hz-1 kHz, 14% at 1-2 kHz, 10% at 2-4 kHz). A nylon string's energy is its body, and 'six' reads 0.7 dB over the records at 250-500 Hz and 1.3 short at 2-4 kHz; v16 had already turned it down 3 dB for that body. So the section's own idea, six strings for six strokes, was the part of the song least likely to be heard.
WHY A SITAR. (1) It is still six strings (one school of the instrument strings it with six), and its buzz lies where the passage has room: alone it has 8.1 dB less of itself at 250-500 Hz than at 2-4 kHz; the nylon 1.8 dB less. (2) The song already counts five and seven by hand on a tabla (v14, v18); six lay between them with a Spanish guitar. (3) THE STRINGS WERE ALREADY TUNED TO IT. F, G flat, A flat, B, C, F is Sa, flat Re, flat Ga, sharp Ma, Pa, Sa, and the tap's E over the cadence is the Ni: every note sounding in 'six' is a note of Todi, with only its sixth missing. Nobody chose that; the riff's two answers did.
BENCHED on the same notes at the same fader (K against everything else over its fourteen beats; its share of the passage at 250-500 Hz / at 2-4 kHz): the nylon -11.7, 19% / 10%; the library's steel-string acoustic -12.4, 9% / 11% (it lives above 8 kHz); its six-string guitar -10.3, 41% / 11% (all body); its clean funk guitar -20.4; the sitar -8.2, 12% / 26%.
THE SITAR AS KEPT. The library's rings on: 12 dB down half a beat after its last stroke, into the cadence, where the guitar stopped dead. Here its release is 400 ms (24 dB down at the same point), its hall is halved, and its top is rolled off (as it comes it is a third of the passage's 4-8 kHz). Fader -10 dB (the nylon's was -11). It stands 8.8 dB under everything else while it sounds (11.1 before; the tap in the same bars 8.4) and holds 14, 36, 16, 25 and 16% of the passage in the five bands from 250 Hz to 8 kHz. IN TUNE: its F3 sounds 1.2 to 1.8 cents over the note on each of its first eight harmonics (the nylon's same string -9.9 to +5.6). The return in A flat, at -7 dB as before, stands 5.7 under (7.8).
THE READ, 'six' against the eleven records' passages with no voice (this song has none): 0.500 -> 0.411, and its own ten seconds 0.544 -> 0.422. By band: 250-500 Hz +0.7 -> +0.3 and 2-4 kHz -1.3 -> -0.9 (what the swap was for); 500 Hz-1 kHz 0.0 -> +0.3 and 4-8 kHz +0.2 -> +0.4 (what it costs). 'A flat' 0.411 -> 0.411.
WHAT IT COSTS, AND WHAT I DOUBT. (1) A sitar in a djent song is a colour some will hear as a postcard. The tabla was there first and the tuning was there before either; that is my case, and an ear may still say no. (2) It is a third of the passage's 500 Hz-1 kHz now: if it reads as nasal there, that band is where. (3) It plays a guitarist's figure, a pass straight across the strings, not a sitar's: no slide, no drone string, no ornament. I left those out on purpose (a rule in the motifs board): the swap is the instrument, and anything more wants an ear. (4) Whether the pass still GROWS audibly, one string to six over seven beats, I cannot measure: a buzzing string may blur the count the nylon kept clean (a stroke falls 2.5 dB before the next; the nylon's fell 3.0). (5) Two of v16's bench figures in the generator's comment are now history (they were the nylon's).
FINISHED FILES, three seeds: the strings' ten seconds +0.20 to +0.23 dB; every other section -0.011 to -0.022 dB with nothing else in it (residual -60 to -75 dB; 'A flat' +0.00 to +0.01). WHY. The song gives every speed a guest (the open hat at two, the bell and the foot at three, the baritone and clavinet at four, the tabla at five, the sitar at six), and none of them is a harmony. For most of its first two minutes every pitched part plays the riff's five notes in unison or octaves. At three to the beat four guitars played the same seven strokes for twenty seconds, and chirper-zero's cross-beat (v4), which is the passage's whole idea, is a thing of timing that a wall of unison does nothing to set off.
THE IDEA. Three, so thirds. Each answer gets the note a third above it IN THE SONG'S OWN SIX NOTES (F, G flat, A flat, B, C, E flat: two steps up the scale), played an octave up by the second pair while the main pair and the bass keep the answer itself. Because the scale is uneven the thirds are not alike: A flat-C and B-E flat are major tenths, G flat-B and C-F are elevenths. So the riff's two cells, which differed by one semitone in each answer, now differ in kind. The six notes turn out to hold three triads a minor third apart (F minor, A flat major, B major), and the lifted answers spell the last two against the F the cell opens on. Then the answers climb: for the last four cells the right guitar plays its thirds an octave higher (C4, E flat 4, B3, F4), reaching the clavinet's notes (B3, C4) just as 'four' hands the answers to the guests (v2). WHY A TANPURA, AND WHY THERE. Every speed in this song has a guest of its own, and from five on they all come from one music: a tabla counts the fives (v14), a sitar's six strings the sixes (chirper-two's v28), the tabla again the sevens (v18). That music does not begin with its drum or its string. It begins with the drone, which is there before anybody plays and never changes. This song has one thing that never changes too: the beat. So where the band comes in, a tanpura comes in and PLAYS THE BEAT: four strings, one to a beat, Pa Sa Sa Sa, so its cycle is exactly the bar the kit keeps. It goes seven times round while the riff goes eight times round its seven strokes: four against seven, the song's two numbers, on the instrument whose whole job is to stay put. Two notes, for the speed of two: the F the riff stands on and the C its second answer reaches. v28 found that every note the riff plays is a note of Todi; this is the drone that scale is sung over, and the riff's G flat and B now lean on a held F and C, which is what those two notes are for in that music.
AND 'TWO' WAS THE EMPTIEST STRETCH OF THE SONG: two guitars, a bass, a bass drum on every stroke and a hat. Its guest was the open hat. By the read (the mix beside the records' passages with no voice; nobody sings in this song) it stood furthest from the records of all nine stretches but 'one': 1.600, short by 2.8 dB at 250-500 Hz, 1.3 at 500 Hz-1 kHz, 1.1 at 1-2 kHz.
IT COMES FIRST: the cycle's last two strings are plucked alone in the last two beats of the opening (3 dB softer), over the clean guitars' C and F, so the first thing the tanpura does is complete the fifth the riff's own answer began. Each guitar has a figure seven beats long: an open F, four muted strokes, and two answers side by side. The right has A flat and B; the left has G flat and C. v1 called the answers "the album hook in two bites": each bite is now said whole by one guitar, on one side, at the opening's pace.
